newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia, China, C.Asian states strike border deal.
newsitem.headline: Russia, China, C.Asian states strike border deal.

text.p: The presidents of Russia, China, Kazakhstan, Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan on Thursday signed a pact on troop reductions along the former Sino-Soviet border which they hope will set an example on how to maintain regional security.

"This day will go down in history," Russia's Boris Yeltsin told China's Jiang Zemin, Kyrgyzstan's Askar Akayev, Kazakhstan's Nursultan Nazarbayev and Imomali Rakhmonov of Tajikistan before the signing ceremony.
"It took us seven years of tense talks to reach this result, which is unprecedented for Asia and the Pacific region," he added.
Border clashes in 1969 marked the climax of hostility between the Soviet Union and China, whose alliance of the 1950s had collapsed into rivalry for leadership of the communist world.
Relations between Beijing and Moscow have been gradually improving since 1989 and the independent states left by the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991 have establed friendly relations with China.
No details of the treaty have been offically disclosed.

But Interfax news agency quoted Russian government experts as saying the pact would set limits to land forces, short-range aviation and anti-aircraft defences deployed in a 100-km (63-mile) wide strip along the border which stretches for more than 7,000 km (4,400 miles).
The experts said the treaty would not affect strategic missile forces, long-range aviation and navy deployed in the area. It sets special limits for border troops.
The pact, which also includes a system of mutual inspections to make the 100-km strip transparent, is to be ratified by the parliaments of the five signatories.

"This is a good example of how to solve tricky and delicate national security issues through building up mutual confidence rather than by building up troops and expanding military blocs," Itar-Tass news agency quoted a Russian Foreign Ministry official as saying.

Interfax also quoted Russian military experts as saying that, under the deal, China may have up to 3,900 tanks in the security zone along the border -- as many as the other four signatories put together. Russia would dominate the non-Chinese share with 3,810 tanks.
The sources told Interfax Russia would cut its forces in the zone by 15 percent. They gave no absolute figures.
"There will be no vacuum on the border because the aim of the treaty is to establish a calm, good-neighbourly and friendly atmosphere among the signatories rather than to weaken them," Yeltsin said.
"There will be enough troops in the 100-km zones to ensure the security of Russia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan on the one side and China on the other."
The signing ceremony in Moscow followed talks on Wednesday between Yeltsin and Jiang which were crowned by a declaration outlining their vision of a post-Cold War world with no dominant superpower.

"No country should seek hegemony, practise power politics or monopolise international affairs," the declaration said without mentioning any specific country but clearly with the United States in mind.

Russia has snuggled up to China since its honeymoon with the West ended over NATO's decision to offer membership to some eastern European countries, which Moscow sees this as a threat to its security.
But some Russian newspapers expressed doubts about the reproachement with China.
"So far it is difficult to say whether we need to recklessly plunge into a new alliance with the East just because we are not getting a proper hearing in the West," Nezavisimaya Gazeta daily said.
The liberal daily Sevodnya questioned Moscow's plans to boost arms sales to China, saying the decision could cause problems for Russia in the future.
"Why do we need to arm our neighbour, who exceeds us by at least eight times in population?" the newspaper asked.
Both countries have made clear they will not be driven back into the closeness of the 1950s and want instead to forge a "strategic partnership".
